abstract: Lifelong preservation of skeletal muscle function is essential for healthy aging. Sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength, arises from aging itself (primary sarcopenia) or chronic diseases (secondary sarcopenia). Although these forms frequently coexist, whether they share a therapeutically targetable mechanism remains unclear. Here we identify soluble, full-length Delta-like ligand 4 (Dll4), released from endothelial cells, as a common driver of both forms of sarcopenia. Endothelium-derived Dll4 increases with age and accumulates in interstitial spaces through binding to type I collagen, where it selectively activates Notch2. Chronic Dll4 exposure impairs muscle function, induces endothelial senescence, and promotes vascular regression. Conversely, sustained Dll4 inhibition attenuates primary sarcopenia, preserves vascular integrity, ameliorates systemic aging phenotypes, and extends lifespan, even when initiated in aged mice. Studies in human cohorts and mouse models further uncover a kidney-vascular-muscle axis linking renal dysfunction to elevated circulating Dll4, whose blockade prevents secondary sarcopenia. Together, these findings indicate that endothelium-released Dll4 acts as a shared mediator of primary and secondary sarcopenia and systemic aging, highlighting its inhibition as a promising strategy to extend healthspan and lifespan.
